title: String Theory and Phase: Mathematical Correspondence and Current Interpretation

summary: We study unitary \(S^1\)-manifolds with four isolated fixed points in relation to Kosniowski's conjectural inequality \(4χ(M)>\dim M\). For every integer \(m\ge3\), we show that there exists a unitary \(S^1\)-manifold \(M_m^{18}\) with exactly four isolated fixed points, and these manifolds are pairwise distinct and nonzero in ordinary complex bordism. Since \(χ(M_m^{18})=4\), they give an infinite family of counterexamples to \(4χ(M)>\dim M\). By gluing two blocks formed by \(G_2/SU(3)\cong S^6\) and the unit disk $D(V)$ of 12- dimensional real $S^1$-representation $V$ along their equivariantly identified free boundaries, we explicitly construct such a manifold $M^{18}_3$. We also prove that the four-point case is null-bordant in real dimension \(16\) and in every real dimension greater than \(18\); hence \(18\) is the smallest dimension in which such a counterexample occurs.
title: Unitary $S^1$-Manifolds with Four Fixed Points and Kosniowski's Conjecture

summary: Recent large audio language models (LALMs) have extended their capabilities beyond lexical speech understanding to tasks requiring paralinguistic and non-linguistic audio understanding, such as emotion recognition. However, these models still struggle to reliably utilize acoustic information, particularly when it co-occurs with spoken linguistic content. Existing benchmarks do not clearly distinguish acoustic perception from higher-level reasoning, making it difficult to identify the source of these failures. To address this issue, we introduce VocalGrad, a benchmark designed to evaluate LALMs' ability to perceive low-level acoustic variations. VocalGrad formulates this problem as a simple binary classification of temporal change direction, enabling evaluation largely independent of higher-level reasoning or semantic understanding. Our benchmark results reveal a substantial gap in acoustic perception between human annotators and state-of-the-art LALMs: while human annotators achieve high accuracy, LALMs perform at near-chance levels. We further conduct linear probing to identify structural bottlenecks in these models. Our analysis reveals two distinct failure modes: for some categories, task-relevant information is preserved in internal representations but not utilized by the language model head; for others, the information becomes progressively less linearly decodable across model layers. Overall, our results reveal substantial limitations of LALMs in modeling acoustic variation under controlled settings and expose representation differences not observable from text outputs.
title: VocalGrad: Evaluating Acoustic Perception in Audio Language Models

summary: Physical plausibility is essential for realistic video generation. Existing methods impose physical guidance before synthesis via simulations or refined prompts, but this can limit dynamic diversity, miss errors that emerge only after generation, and require repeated regeneration when inconsistencies remain. We therefore study a generate-diagnose-repair paradigm that preserves the original generation capability and selectively repairs physical inconsistencies afterward, raising two key questions: what to repair and how to repair? To address them, we introduce PhysRepair, an agentic video generation framework that combines causal reasoning over the observed physical failure with prior repair experience to enable localized and adaptive correction. Specifically, Spatiotemporal Causal Constraints identify the first invalid physical state and its causally affected states, producing a repair specification that guides physically plausible local regeneration while preserving unaffected content. Experience-augmented In-context Learning combines the ongoing repair context with relevant experience from previous repairs, allowing the agent to adapt its repair decisions across diverse physical failures and accumulate completed trajectories for future cases. Experiments on Physics-IQ Verified across solid mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, thermodynamics, and magnetism demonstrate that PhysRepair consistently improves the physical plausibility of generated videos over existing methods. Our project page is available at https://xxkkxxx.github.io/PhysRepair-Website/.
title: Agentic Physics-Grounded Video Generation via Memory-Augmented In-Context Reasoning

summary: Diffusion-based multimodal large language models (dMLLMs) decode by iterative denoising with bidirectional attention, which precludes the standard autoregressive key--value cache. Practical deployments therefore rely on approximate caching that reuses intermediate states across denoising steps. Such caching, however, often makes a response repeat one token at adjacent positions in a run that breaks the sentence, a failure we term the \emph{Repeat Curse}. Tracing the context-token information flow reveals three disruptions. Within a step, caching disperses the attention that anchors a position on nearby context tokens. Across steps, similarity-based refresh is not staleness-aware, so some positions are decoded against stale key--value states. Across layers, the deep-layer entropy of the context fails to converge where repetition arises. We accordingly propose CoTA++, a training-free, plug-and-play framework that counteracts each disruption where it originates: Context-Token Attention Re-anchoring re-forms the attention routing against the current context, Decode-Aware Refresh reserves part of the cache's refresh budget for the positions about to be committed, and Context-Token Entropy-Guided Voting discounts the confidence of a position by the deep-layer entropy of its context, which reorders the unmasking. The three components act at non-overlapping stages of a decoding step and compose freely with existing dMLLMs and caches. Across three dMLLMs and two caching backends, CoTA++ reduces the sample repetition rate of long responses from up to 99.6\% to at most 17.0\%, recovers most of the accuracy lost to caching on nine benchmarks, and keeps the speedup of caching at under 15\% overhead, making approximate caching reliable for dMLLMs.
title: CoTA++: Understanding the Repeat Curse in dMLLMs from an Information Flow Perspective

summary: LLM agents increasingly use retrieval tools across languages, yet their safety evaluation remains English-centric. It remains unclear whether language affects tool admission, post-retrieval generation, or both. We independently vary request, retrieved-page, and required response languages in a controlled URL-retrieval setting across ten models and seven languages. We identify Safety Loss through Interlingual Processing (SLIP). Non-English harmful requests increase mean tool admission from 46.9% to 67.4%, with a positive mean change in every model. This pattern also persists in an autonomous retrieval setup across all four models tested in this setting. Requiring answers in the page language increases pooled harmfulness on matched tool calls from 50.3% to 57.4% across four closed-weight models, mainly in Chinese and Hindi. Translating pages alone produces no consistent harm increase in eight models with comparable inference settings. Automated audits show that a non-harmful response may be a genuine safety refusal, a deflection citing language difficulties, or an unusable answer. Harmfulness labels alone cannot distinguish these outcomes. Multilingual safety evaluations should therefore measure tool admission and response harmfulness separately and distinguish refusal from capability failure.
title: Disentangling Language Effects on Tool Admission and Post-Retrieval Safety

summary: The microscopic origin of chirality induced spin selectivity (CISS) in biomolecular structures has traditionally been discussed in terms of spin orbit coupling and spin angular momentum. However, orbital angular momentum (OAM) is increasingly recognized as a more direct electronic response to molecular chirality. A helical hopping network built only from s orbitals can support an itinerant orbital moment and an orbital Edelstein response, but such a basis has no local atomic OAM and therefore omits the complementary contribution arising from coherence among active p orbitals. Here we construct a six-band multiorbital double helix model parameterized by characteristic B form DNA geometry and hopping scales. The model incorporates major minor groove asymmetry, an axial base pair offset representing stagger, and compositional inequivalence between the two strands, providing structural control parameters with which the orbital response can be tuned. Inter strand hybridization generates a full three component atomic OAM texture in the corotating local helical frame, including a radial component absent in the corresponding single helix model. We separately evaluate the itinerant OAM using the Bloch wave packet formulation of orbital magnetization and identify an additional inter-strand circulation channel unique to the double-helix connectivity. The resulting atomic and itinerant responses have distinct microscopic origins, magnitudes, and temperature dependences, establishing a multiorbital framework for geometry controlled angular momentum generation and transport in chiral molecular conductors.
title: Orbital Angular Momentum Currents and Textures in a Multiorbital Double Helix

summary: Quantum kernels are among the most promising methods in quantum machine learning, providing a natural way to embed data into high-dimensional Hilbert spaces via quantum circuits and capturing non-linear relationships in data. Their learning behaviour is governed by the function class they represent, which is formally characterized by the structure of the associated Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). However, a theoretical characterization of this function class, and of how it depends on the choice of feature map and its hyperparameters, is still lacking. In this work, we focus on the Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial (IQP) feature map and derive a Fourier representation of the associated RKHS generators as finite sums of trigonometric functions evaluated on polynomially transformed input variables, with a finite set of accessible frequencies determined by the circuit construction and scaled by the bandwidth hyperparameter. This representation identifies three bandwidth regimes with qualitatively distinct expressive properties from localised, through multimodal, to periodic. Numerical experiments on synthetic datasets with controlled periodic and multimodal structure, across data dimensions and feature-map configurations, reproduce the three regimes in both supervised classification and unsupervised anomaly detection, benchmarked against a classical Gaussian kernel. These results make the relationship between expressivity and data structure explicit for IQP kernels: expressive power translates into a practical benefit only when the accessible frequencies match with the structure of the data, which provides a criterion for selecting the bandwidth when the periodic or multimodal structure of data is known.
title: Expressivity of IQP Feature-Map Quantum Kernels via Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces

summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine, with the source, the Lean development and the checks of the paper BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI by D. Bhattacharjee and U. Bhattacharya. The engine is the Python package eBLLM (command anaxia ), a Lean 4 library and the container image ghcr.io/creelie/bllm-engine, which carries no model weights. The paper proves, in a model with independent runs, that certifying self-modifications costs an entropy (the entropy law), that a sound infinite self-improvement of finite cost exists exactly when one series converges, that a proposer needs a number of proposals set by a Rényi entropy of order one half, and that n verified layers sharing one budget cost at least n log(n/θ). Sixty-five of its theorems are proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib, each depending only on the three standard axioms. The engine combines known constructions in a typed crossing network with a program check and a refuter for every candidate, a shared memory and five target agents, and builds new objects in construction mode: a goal-directed builder and an exists-forall search, each followed by an independent gate. From the rules of Steinberg's problem it rebuilds the gadgets of the 2016 counterexample of Cohen-Addad, Hebdige, Král', Li and Salgado; it finds nothing on Erdős's question for cycles of length 4 to 6. Layer towers of depth one to three, a ladder and a mesh, are compared with the crossing loop at the same number of checks. A Hodge-only run of twelve rounds leaves every target point at the same gap. None of the five benchmark problems (the lattice Yang–Mills mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, the standard conjecture of Lefschetz type, Chowla's conjecture, Erdős problem 1183) is solved. The registry of the systems, methods and collections the engine draws on, with what it takes from each and what it leaves, is src/ebllm/bllm/data/sources.json and Appendix D of the paper.
title: BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI

summary: Long-horizon GUI agents rely on visual history to maintain task states, but retaining historical screenshots increases visual-token usage and inference costs, while textual summaries can discard critical state information, undermining long-horizon reliability. We propose ECHOES, which leverages training-time privileged information to guide textual history compression and strengthen long-horizon reasoning. Specifically, ECHOES adopts a Compression-Think-Action (CTA) format to recursively update a textual history state and reason. The same model, given privileged multi-image inputs, serves as a teacher that provides dense token-level on-policy distillation on student-generated CTA rollouts. Our Perception-Memory Fidelity (PMF) Gap-guided OPD-RL framework dynamically balances privileged distillation and task-reward optimization, with periodic teacher updates supporting continued improvement. We further introduce ECHOESBMK, a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark derived from real GUI agent failure trajectories to jointly evaluate visual perception and cross-modal state retention. Experiments on four GUI benchmarks and ECHOESBMK demonstrate substantial gains in task performance and memory fidelity. Without retaining historical screenshots at deployment, ECHOES achieves competitive performance with a favorable performance-inference-cost trade-off and exhibits positive zero-shot transfer to unseen visual planning tasks.
title: ECHOES: Seeing Beyond the Current Image via Recursive History Compression and Privileged On-Policy Distillation

summary: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. We study this question in agentic video understanding, where rich multimodal evidence and coupled mechanisms make harness optimization challenging. We first introduce VHarness-BRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that evolves video harnesses around a frozen vision-language model. Analyzing over 4,000 evolved candidates, we find it competitive with hand-engineered systems but identify three interconnected failure modes: validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap. We trace all three to a common root: the same imperfect validation evidence drives both harness revisions and the proposer's search strategy. We therefore propose VHarness-SRSI, an evidence-governed framework in which every search decision rests on evidence that is transferable, sufficient, and gathered before the search commits. It restricts the proposer to content-free feedback, informs exploration with instrumented warm-up experiments, and develops mechanisms in isolated probe-race branches before factorial composition and joint refinement. Across four video understanding benchmarks, VideoHarness-SRSI improves the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to VideoHarness-BRSI and reduces the mean validation-test gap by 37.9%. Reliable harness evolution thus depends on how search is organized and informed, not only on how well it optimizes validation performance.
title: VideoHarness-SRSI: Structured Recursive Self-Improvement for Video Understanding Harness

summary: Future quantum networks will rely on control-plane decisions such as routing, scheduling, entanglement provisioning, purification, and memory allocation. Each decision depends on a timely and reliable estimate of the quality of the entanglement that a candidate path can deliver, with end-to-end fidelity as a central metric. Inspired by the optical-networking experience with quality-of-transmission (QoT) estimation, this article asks when a quantum controller should compute fidelity analytically, simulate it, or learn a surrogate model. The optical analogy is useful but incomplete: optical QoT estimation often predicts a scalar transmission margin, whereas quantum QoT estimation must account for probabilistic entanglement generation, random memory waiting times, decoherence, state consumption, and measurement constraints that can make fidelity a stochastic target. We propose a compute/simulate/learn framework for quantum QoT estimation and illustrate it with a simulation-based proof of concept. Our study shows that analytical composition can be sufficient in simple regimes, that simulation becomes necessary when stochastic memory effects shape the delivered fidelity distribution, and that lightweight learned surrogates can approximate simulator labels at much lower runtime cost for online control. We close with open challenges for deployment, including stochastic targets, sim-to-real transfer, data-generation cost, physics-informed learning, and generalization beyond individual paths to full network topologies.
title: Quality-of-Transmission Estimation in Quantum Networks: Compute, Simulate, or Learn?

summary: Long-term memory enables language-model agents to personalize future interactions, but a finite memory bank cannot preserve every extracted fact. Existing memory gating policies are typically shared across users and therefore fail to account for user-specific patterns of future reuse. In this paper, we study memory gating at the fact level. We first propose a retrieval-based labeling strategy that labels each fact by whether it is later retrieved and incorporated into responses. We then formulate online memory gating as contextual apple tasting with delayed one-sided feedback, and propose Warm-Start UCB, which combines offline learning from existing data with online adaptation to the current user. Our theoretical analysis establishes a high-probability regret upper bound of $\tilde{O}(Tε\wedge d\sqrt{T})$ when the delay window is at most $O(\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ is the total number of rounds, $ε$ is the initialization error, $d$ is the dimension of the feature map, and $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ hides constant and poly-logarithmic factors. The results of our experiment demonstrate that our method outperforms all baselines under different memory budgets and history lengths, establishing it as a promising personalized memory gating policy.
title: Learning Personalized Memory Gating from Delayed One-Sided Feedback

summary: Latent world models learn action-conditioned state transitions in a compact representation space, providing a predictive model for visual planning and control. However, planning with these models typically requires costly test-time optimization over action sequences. We propose to replace this online search with a goal-conditioned inverse model that directly predicts actions from current and goal observations. A key challenge is that action prediction alone neither ensures that goal representations encode action-relevant information nor that predicted actions are consistent with the learned latent prediction model. We introduce Hindsight Inverse JEPA Planning (HIJP), a search-free framework that addresses both aspects during training. HIJP relabels future observations along offline trajectories as goals, providing action supervision across multiple temporal horizons. By retaining gradients through the goal representations, this supervision directly shapes the visual representation. HIJP further feeds predicted actions into the latent predictor model and aligns the resulting next-state representations with encoded successor observations, enforcing action-transition consistency. At inference time, the inverse dynamics model and latent predictor models are applied alternately to generate multi-step action sequences without online search. Across four visual control tasks, HIJP achieves 86.8% overall success and a 1.9-16.5x planning speedup over search-based planning.
title: Beyond Action Prediction: Learning Search-Free Planning in Latent Space

summary: Time-aware retrieval is crucial for long-horizon LLM agents to effectively leverage ever-growing long-term memory. Existing methods focus on lexical or semantic similarity, leading to target memories being crowded out by temporally mismatched yet semantically similar candidates. Even time-aware approaches inject temporal cues only during memory organization or answer generation, overlooking temporal constraints at the retrieval stage, where candidate selection occurs - the root cause of the displacement. Inspired by the temporal contiguity effect in human episodic memory, we propose TIDER (Temporal Interval-driven Dual-channel Evidence Retrieval), a time-aware agentic retrieval framework. Central to TIDER is a reinforcement learning (RL)-trained temporal interval locator that infers the temporal windows in which the evidence lies. RL optimizes window localization as a discrete, non-differentiable retrieval decision, using composite rewards to convert sparse answer supervision into fine-grained retrieval feedback. These temporal windows first define the temporal retrieval channel; the retrieved candidates are then merged with results from the semantic channel and reranked by proximity to the windows. This temporal grounding enables TIDER to retrieve temporally aligned evidence that would otherwise be drowned out by the volume of semantically similar yet temporally mismatched memories. With a lightweight 1.7B locator, TIDER achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on both long-horizon memory benchmarks - 61.52% on LifeBench (+8.82%) and 78.96% on LoCoMo (+3.66%) - which indicates that temporal cues are crucial for pinpointing target evidence amid a vast pool of semantically similar historical events in long-term daily-life memory.
title: RL-Guided Temporal Localization for Dual-Channel Retrieval in Long-Horizon Agent Memory

summary: While Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across complex tasks, they predominantly operate in isolated sessions, lacking the ability to continually learn from historical interactions or adapt to user-specific environments. Existing self-evolution paradigms often indiscriminately inject raw interaction trajectories into memory or skill modules, leading to obscured behavioral patterns and compromised update controllability. Furthermore, as foundational LLM reasoning improves, the bottleneck for agentic evolution shifts from accumulating generic knowledge to effectively managing situational experience. To address this, we propose Darwin-Claw, an environment-adaptive self-evolving framework that systematically distills episodic experiences to drive the comprehensive evolution of operational skills and durable memory. Theoretically grounded in an iterative agent-actor and evolver-critic co-adaptation, Darwin-Claw introduces a Hierarchical Experience Consolidation System that extracts fine-grained error attributions and generalizes them into dynamically updated prototype vectors. This structured situational experience serves as interaction patches for context-sensitive perception and explicit optimization signals for skill refinement. Practically, Darwin-Claw is a readily deployable, automated framework compatible with mainstream agent systems without requiring manual curation. Extensive experiments on WildClawBench demonstrate that Darwin-Claw yields substantial performance improvements, establishing a controllable and stable pathway for the continual, user-centric adaptation of autonomous agents in real-world ecosystems.
title: Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents

summary: The recurrent neural network transducer (RNN-T) remains a practical choice for streaming speech recognition, but training requires large intermediate tensors. We present Flash RNN-T, a joint and loss implementation combining specialized kernels with optional tiled recomputation over the full alignment space and vocabulary. Tiled and untiled Flash form the entire measured throughput-memory frontier on medium and long workloads. On H100, untiled Flash achieves 24-39% higher throughput with 26-56% less memory than the fastest baseline on these workloads wherever it fits. Tiling reduces memory further through recomputation. On medium, tiled Flash uses ninefold less memory than that baseline at 16% lower throughput when both use one backward call per batch. On long, it fits where all tested alternatives with that backward schedule run out of memory with 80 GB. These comparisons use each implementation's lowest-memory configuration reaching at least 95% of its peak throughput.
title: Flash RNN-T: Memory-Efficient Joint Network and Transducer Loss Computation

summary: Rapid progress in embodied intelligence has enabled increasingly capable robots to follow language instructions and manipulate diverse objects. However, strong results in structured environments do not automatically transfer to open-world conditions, where clutter, occlusion, and changing viewpoints can obscure the spatial relationships required for action. To address this perceptual gap, a virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced. AWAM, an Active World-Action Model actively plans where to observe and imagines what will be seen along the planned trajectory before acting. Task-related virtual camera motion is predicted and used as a structured query into a geometry-conditioned world model, producing a reusable spatial prior for manipulation, which is later compressed into a fixed memory and fused with live observations through cross-attention for diffusion-based action prediction. AWAM achieves competitive success rates with 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5% on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials. These results support improved robustness to the evaluated occlusions and distribution shifts, addressing part of the gap between structured manipulation and less controlled environments.
title: AWAM: Active Trajectory-Conditioned View Imagination for Robust Robot Manipulation

summary: Modern deep learning systems increasingly rely on high-dimensional vector operations, in which large input and parameter vectors are repeatedly stored, transferred, and processed. Although substantial research has focused on reducing neural-network model size through pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation, and efficient architectures, the storage, memory-traffic, and communication costs associated with repeatedly presented high-dimensional input vectors remain important practical considerations, particularly in distributed and edge-computing environments. This paper proposes the SETAREH (Sorting-assisted Energy-concentrating Transform for Approximate Representation using Haar wavelets) transform, a Haar-wavelet-based sparsification approach for approximating the inner product between a fixed high-dimensional coefficient vector and successive input vectors. By applying the same sequence of permutations and Haar transforms to both vectors, SETAREH preserves the exact inner product before truncation. It then retains only a subset of the transformed coefficient-input pairs, reducing their representation cost while introducing a controllable approximation error. To evaluate SETAREH, we consider two complementary experimental settings: a synthetic Gaussian-vector baseline and a real apparent-age estimation task using a convolutional neural network on the APPA-REAL dataset. The results show that SETAREH can approximate the evaluated inner products using substantially fewer transformed coefficient-input pairs than the original vector dimension. The findings support its use as a potential structured data-representation method for repeated inner products with fixed weights, while the practical benefit depends on approximation accuracy and the cost of storing or transmitting permutation metadata.
title: SETAREH Transform: A Sorting-Assisted Haar-Wavelet Sparsification Method for Approximate Inner-Product Computation

summary: Long-term agent memory requires recovering answer-relevant evidence dispersed across turns and sessions. Existing systems increasingly use structured memories and adaptive retrieval, yet often pass retrieved or expanded units directly to the reader, coupling memory addressing with evidence presentation and leaving the final context redundant or incomplete. To address this gap, we propose MemCompile, a query-conditioned evidence compilation framework for long-term conversational memory. Given a query, the Address Plane locates relevant support through compact source-linked descriptors and capacity-aware Cells, while a normalization boundary resolves heterogeneous retrieval hits to stable SourcePacket identities. Its Evidence Plane then allocates a bounded evidence budget across complementary packets, admits limited additional support, and renders the retained claims associated with each selected packet into an answer-ready context. MemCompile achieves 80.52% Judge Accuracy on LoCoMo and extends the empirical quality-cost Pareto frontier to a higher-quality regime. Its strong performance on LongMemEval-S further suggests that the benefits of query-conditioned compilation generalize across long-term conversational-memory benchmarks.
title: From Memory Hits to Answerable Evidence: Query-Conditioned Memory Compilation for Long-Term Agent Memory

summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent outputs that lack source support or conflict with local operational constraints. We introduce Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT), a modular architecture that organizes generation as a closed Retrieve--Reflect--Revise loop. SRCoT separates environment state, persistent knowledge, accumulated experience, and short-term memory into provenance-labeled stores. BM25 retrieval supplies local context; subsequent passes expose intermediate drafts, missing-information markers, follow-up queries, and optional claim--evidence mappings. These artifacts inform retrieval, revision, clarification, or abstention decisions. We examine the architecture through qualitative, trace-based case studies in two fully synthetic settings: emergency medical services and Munich-Sim, an emergency-operations simulation. Local prototype runs on an Apple M4-family laptop with 128 GB memory illustrate source-labeled documentation, explicit gap marking, and structured dispatch-style outputs. The traces also reveal provenance-assignment errors, incomplete evidence coverage, and unsafe assumptions that remain possible despite prompting constraints. These cases demonstrate report-level inspectability and local execution, not comparative superiority, hallucination reduction, clinical validity, or operational safety. The architecture separates retrieval and control from the model interface, but behavior across different models remains to be evaluated. SRCoT is a research proof of concept requiring human review, with its principal contribution lying in an inspectable control procedure rather than a new model.
title: Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT): Evidence-Based Text Generation via a Closed-Loop Retrieve--Reflect--Revise Pipeline on Edge LLMs

summary: A key challenge in on-policy distillation (OPD) is extracting effective supervision from teacher knowledge. Supervision from token probabilities may underutilize internal knowledge, while direct hidden-state matching forces the student to shift to the teacher's feature space and complicates cross-architecture transfer. Inspired by contrastive learning's use of relationships between instances, we propose \textbf{SimOPD} to transfer teacher internal knowledge through response similarities. Specifically, SimOPD uses paired memory banks of student-generated responses to extract supervision from the teacher's internal representations as similarity distributions. The student then matches these distributions within its own representation space, retaining representational freedom and removing the need for cross-model projection. Extensive experiments show that SimOPD improves the overall average over the strongest baselines by up to 2.6 and 3.1 percentage points in same- and cross-architecture settings.
title: SimOPD: Relational Knowledge Transfer for On-Policy Distillation

summary: LLM-agent memory selection often uses retrieval rankings based on record relevance or individual influence. Such rankings cannot identify sufficient subsets under redundant or jointly necessary evidence. We study per-decision memory sufficiency: selecting a small subset that preserves full-memory behavior. To separate search error from model error, we introduce JointCoreBench, a benchmark with nine interaction families, six workflow domains, natural-language decisions, and exact sufficient-set oracles, and JointCore, a relevance cost-ordered group-deletion baseline that tests blocks before individual records. On 6,912 exact conditions, cost-ordered JointCore recovers a minimum-cost sufficient set in 100.0% of cases, reduces subset evaluations from 30.00 to 11.13 (62.9%), and achieves 87.8% active-memory savings. Across four 12B-70B model families and 432 tasks per model, its unweighted mean is 10.28 versus 16.00 model queries and 50.6% versus 43.1% minimum-cost recovery relative to cost aware singleton deletion. Both methods preserve full-memory behavior under the deterministic primary interface. Tests with physical deletion, UNKNOWN masks, PENDING sentinels, counterfactual values, and alternative labels identify interface dependent behavior. JointCore is an efficient benchmark baseline; the study does not establish deployment-ready memory compression.
title: Beyond Marginal Influence: Interaction-Aware Memory Selection for LLM Agents

summary: Which biological findings enter a reported explanation depends on how the model population was constructed, a choice predictive validation alone does not reveal. We fitted 10,000 L2-regularised logistic regression models to TCGA pan-cancer tumour-versus-normal data: 100 regularisation strengths on 100 train-test splits, with patients fixed within each split. Strongly and weakly regularised models differ in mean accuracy by only 0.21 percentage points, yet prioritise different genes systematically with regularisation strength. Averaging explanations across a hyperparameter grid produces a top-50 panel sharing 41 genes with a single fitted model, but which model depends on the grid centre (Spearman correlation 0.92, 350 simulated practitioners). For 43 of 50 practitioners, the panel combines genes from strongly and weakly regularised models more fully than any fitted model: the explanation belongs to no model whose accuracy was established. A conventional grid recovers only a quarter of genes favoured exclusively by the strongest regularisation. HMGCS2 ranks among the top 50 in 73 of 100 strongly regularised fits and no weakly regularised fits, yet appears in none of 50 simulated reports. Reconstructing a published biomarker workflow on 20 cohort resamples reveals a different failure: the closest refit contains only 23 of the averaged panel's 50 genes, and no panel gene appears in all 20 refits. We define model-relative provenance as how much of a panel any single fitted model contains, distinct from workflow provenance recording how an analysis was run. We provide measurements to make the model population, the choice that selects from it, and that provenance reportable.
title: Same Accuracy, Different Gene Panels: How the Hyperparameter Grid Chooses the Reported Explanation

summary: Real-time inference on small devices needs low activation memory without extra latency, which makes operator order the most valuable memory lever: it is free in time. We show that the usual way of deploying a better order, handing it back to the compiler and regenerating code, is unreliable. In PyTorch Inductor the regenerated program misses its predicted peak in 22 of 54 CPU configurations. It is worse than the stock program in 9 of them and in 19 of 50 on a GPU, and on the GPU it also changes numerical results. We instead profile the generated program, model its memory exactly from its own statements and their read/write effects, and permute those statements. We prove that this realizes the modeled peak whenever allocation does not depend on history. It does so to the byte, with bitwise-identical results, in all our CPU runs. On the GPU we characterize why the caching allocator breaks the condition. To know when to stop, we give forward and reverse "trap" lower bounds, each computable with $O(n^2)$ minimum cuts. They certify the found order optimal for 94% of held-out wrapper graphs and all 16 microcontroller-class models we study, in under a second. So most inference graphs are already scheduled optimally. Branching networks are the exception, where reordering is free and pays, e.g. 10.0% on DeepLabV3. In compiled training we save up to 7.6%. Beyond the certified optimum we study selective recomputation with per-operator caps. It is strongly NP-hard for every fixed cap even at treewidth two, encodes knapsack exactly on series-parallel graphs, and is solvable exactly on bounded treewidth. It is useless on public tiny models whose peak is a single layer, but on architectures that hold a cheap value for a late reuse it pays: on the public ReDimNet speaker networks, whose order is already optimal, it lowers the peak by 5.2-6.1% at under 0.4% extra MACs, with bitwise-identical outputs.
title: Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust: Exact Realization, Certified Optimality, and the Limits of Recomputation for Inference

summary: Outcome-reward reinforcement learning such as GRPO gives every token of a search-agent rollout the same advantage, although the rollout exercises two capabilities: finding evidence and using it. We show that accuracy improves without grounding: Search-R1 raises accuracy on all seven QA benchmarks, yet on Bamboogle the evidence-supported share of correct answers falls from 84.0% to 42.9%. We attribute this to GRPO's credit assignment: rollouts that retrieve answer-bearing evidence are favoured in aggregate only in proportion to their accuracy gain over the rest, a grounding gap that answering from memory or misusing evidence shrinks or reverses. To address this, we propose Grounded Credit Assignment (GCA), which uses verifiable sub-outcomes (evidence retrieval and answer correctness) to correct search and answer credit separately: a wrong answer is blamed more than the search that found the evidence, and a correct answer that bypasses retrievable evidence is credited less. Never negative on evidence-finding search, the correction does not shrink with the grounding gap; capped at 10% of each token's advantage, it never overrides the outcome signal. Without extra models, rollouts, or training stages, GCA improves average EM over Search-R1 by 5.7 (Qwen2.5-3B) and 6.3 points (Qwen3-30B-A3B) and raises this share from 76.9% to 93.4%.
title: Grounded Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Search Agents

summary: In autonomous driving, perceiving surrounding objects is not enough: failing to understand how they move and interact over time can lead to dangerous decisions. Evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) therefore requires testing whether they connect past spatial observations to future consequences. Yet existing benchmarks often assess edge cases through basic perception questions or test temporal understanding in simple scenarios, leaving complex spatiotemporal reasoning underexplored. We introduce STRIDE (SpatioTemporal Reasoning In Driving Edge Cases), an object-centric benchmark for long-tail, safety-critical driving scenarios. STRIDE covers six task families: spatial perception, spatial understanding, temporal memory, temporal extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness. It pairs multiple-choice questions probing individual spatiotemporal judgments with related free-form visual question answering (VQA) requiring detailed scene explanations and justifications of driving decisions. We prioritize scenes with unusual object behaviors and complex traffic interactions, generate reference answers from structured dataset annotations through automated procedures, and use limited language-model assistance and human verification to ensure annotation quality. Across 12 proprietary, open-weight, and driving-specialized models, even the best performer, GPT-6-Astra, achieves only 43.4% average multiple-choice accuracy, versus an approximately 20% random-choice baseline. Further analysis reveals that strong performance in describing driving scenes does not necessarily translate to accurate safety-critical judgments, and that models struggle more with reconstructing object motion than recalling past positions. STRIDE thus exposes spatiotemporal driving limitations that aggregate VQA scores can conceal.
title: STRIDE: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Driving Edge Cases

summary: The linear representation hypothesis holds that pretrained vision models encode generative factors as linearly decodable directions in feature space, and comes with a standard methodology: train a linear probe, declare a factor represented if accuracy is high. We show this test is too permissive. Asymptotically, any sufficiently rich feature map, including a random one, admits a linear readout, so high probe accuracy is consistent with two very different geometries: a true linear world model, where the latent-aligned subspace dominates the representation, or a kernel machine, where the latents lie linearly inside a much larger curved manifold. This distinction matters because the curved structure orthogonal to the probe is relevant for out-of-distribution generalization, robustness, and compositional transfer. We propose three asymmetric diagnostics that distinguish the two cases: reverse predictivity, spectral concentration, and out-of-distribution generalization. We validate them in a fully observed simulation where ground truth is known. Applied to six pretrained vision transformers on SVG-World, our deterministic generative benchmark with paired visual styles, and to two of them on CelebA, they show pretraining produces structure beyond a random kernel but well short of a linear world model. On dSprites, 3D Shapes and MPI3D, forward decodability and latent-aligned variance dissociate. Thus, forward decoding alone does not show that the probed factors align with the dominant geometry of the representation. In summary, our work cautions about the success of linear probes as opposed to truly linear and low dimensional representations.
title: Is a Linear Probe Evidence of a Linear Representation?

summary: Three dimensional modeling for autonomous driving must continuously estimate road geometry, obstacle occupancy, traffic participant behavior, and observational uncertainty under limited computational resources. Existing reconstruction methods can synthesize realistic novel views, but visual fidelity does not sufficiently characterize the geometric reliability required for driving. Generative world models can expand scenarios and predict future observations, yet may introduce content unsupported by measurements. We propose DriveWorld3D, a framework combining temporal video learning, measurement constraints from multiple sensors, and offline generative simulation. Its online component maintains a unified world state comprising road surfaces, volumetric occupancy, dynamic entities, and road relations, while separately representing physical occupancy, observability, and evidence provenance. Action conditioned future prediction and risk sensitive planning connect this representation to driving decisions. Its offline component reconstructs recorded scenes using neural radiance fields or 3D Gaussian Splatting, then expands long tail conditions using generative models while restricting the use of generated content as geometric ground truth. We specify data partitioning, sensor ablations, fault injection, paired closed loop testing, and real to simulation consistency assessment. The central hypothesis is that explicit evidence management can reduce dangerous false free space predictions and occlusion risk within a matched computational budget while retaining acceptable driving efficiency. All performance claims remain subject to experimental validation. Keywords: autonomous driving; 3D occupancy; sensor fusion; uncertainty; generative world models; NeRF; 3D Gaussian Splatting; closed loop simulation
title: DriveWorld3D Evidence Constrained 3D World Modeling and Generative Simulation for Real-World Autonomous Driving

summary: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity through selective lookup, but the full embedding table must remain available for every possible input. We introduce Conditional Program (CP), a compressed representation that reconstructs only the rows an input requests. CP represents each row by a short code and a local scale, with a reconstruction program shared across the table. We instantiate this representation with a Gaussian trellis, norm restoration and independently decodable row records. CP's two-bit code lowers output KL by 41--63\% relative to 2-bit round-to-nearest. Analysis across three trained n-gram memory families shows that Gaussian-like coordinate statistics coexist with learned relationships among rows; at matched storage budgets, the shared trellis outperforms the fitted codebooks and low-rank residual variants we test. For DeepSeek, it reduces table storage from 203GB to 51GB, leaving room for larger workloads when the table is kept on GPU.
title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models

summary: Understanding and simulating how subjective cognition and mental states emerge, evolve, and shape behavior is essential for advancing artificial intelligence toward deeper social cognition and general intelligence. Existing large language models (LLMs) and Theory of Mind (ToM) methods primarily infer mental states from linguistic information, lacking unified mechanisms for subjective world construction, cognitive-psychological interactions, dynamic evolution, and historical dependencies. This paper introduces the Mental World Model (MWM) and its implementation, the Multi-Branch Mental Evolution Architecture (MMEA), which explicitly constructs subjective worlds, models interactions between cognition and mental states, and simulates continuous mental evolution shaped by historical experiences. On DynToM and RecToM, MMEA achieves 96.48% and 94.00% accuracy, respectively, outperforming leading LLMs and specialized ToM methods. Additional experiments demonstrate improvements of 28.7, 39.3, and 16.6 percentage points in mental state and behavior prediction, long-sequence prediction, and implicit mental state inference, respectively. The results demonstrate that MMEA provides an interpretable framework for continuous mental modeling, enabling AI to move beyond surface-level semantic representations to infer individuals' underlying mental states from linguistic information and dynamically simulate their internal cognitive processes and evolution over time. MWM also provides a promising foundation for causal reasoning, personalized AI, sustained human-AI interaction, and future advances toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).
title: Beyond Large Language Models: A Mental World Model Framework for Mental Modeling, Simulation, Evolution, and Interpretability

summary: Optimizing product listings for generative search requires language agents not only to rewrite effectively but also to continually self-improve by retaining successful strategies across diverse categories. However, existing approaches often treat structured listings as free-form text, leaving effective strategies implicit in prompts, search trajectories, or rewritten outputs rather than accumulating them as a reusable agentic memory. To address this limitation, we introduce GLOBE, an agentic framework that drives continual self-improvement by storing optimization knowledge in an evolving handbook of explicit, field-scoped behaviors. In each episode, an Editor applies relevant behaviors and receives rank-based feedback, which a Reflector converts into behavior updates. Crucially for dependable execution in real-world settings, a Moderator removes redundant proposals, a Curator commits accepted changes, and consistently harmful behaviors are deactivated. This cycle transforms episodic feedback into a persistent, field-scoped optimization memory. Experiments show that structured behaviors outperform monolithic prompt optimization, while feedback-driven evolution and moderation further improve effectiveness and reduce downside risk. The learned behaviors also remain effective on unseen product categories, suggesting that agentic memory evolution supports interpretable and transferable product optimization.
title: GLOBE: Evolving Structured Agentic Memory for E-commerce Product Optimization in Generative Search

summary: Users who run a memory-bound OpenFOAM case on an AMD EPYC cluster must decide how many nodes to use and how many MPI ranks to place on each core complex. The fastest choice is often not the cheapest one. This paper revisits our earlier analytical model of this performance and energy trade-off with 560 measured configurations of the motorBike case on five Zen 4 and Zen 5 EPYC processors, including socket power from processor telemetry. On up to four nodes, small meshes are both fastest and cheapest on a single node on most processors. For the largest mesh the largest node count is both the fastest and the cheapest option, because its speedup is superlinear. A genuine trade-off arises only for medium meshes, where full speed costs a median of 20 to 97% more node hours than the cheapest option. The L3 miss rate and the halo traffic per cell are consistent with this pattern. For a new mesh of the same case, the configuration that was optimal on the nearest measured mesh is near optimal in 75 to 85% of the decisions. Running the two configurations it recommends for speed and for cost raises this share to 85 to 90% for runtime and node hours and determines the trade-off with median errors of 3 to 5 percentage points. Neither gradient boosted trees trained on the same data nor the earlier polynomial model improves on this simple procedure.
title: Data-Driven Prediction of Optimal MPI Rank Placement and Node Count for Memory-Bound CFD on AMD EPYC Clusters

summary: When we say that a robot uses memory, does that memory actually play a role? Success-rate ablations alone cannot establish the use of task-relevant facts: they change information and computation together, while aggregate rates can hide offsetting gains and losses. We propose an Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol (IMEP) for vision-language-action (VLA) systems to address four questions: (1) Does memory provide a net benefit? (2) Under what conditions does memory help? (3) Do changes to memory alter task outcomes? (4) Are these effects specific to task-relevant facts? At the retrieval interface, we compare target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal numerical perturbations, and exact replicas, while assessing decision correctness separately from motor execution success. We evaluate within-episode, cross-episode, and agentic memory. In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) intervention, including its installation procedure, changes 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts produces no clear additional effect over fact-preserving replacements. To examine when memory helps, we introduce ChainBench, where correct decisions require historical information unavailable in current observations. The full memory configuration raises task success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under shared recorded executions. These results show that correct history can support robot decisions, but establishing whether a memory system realizes this benefit requires fact-specific evidence beyond aggregate success rates.
title: Beyond Success Rate: Interventional Evaluation of Memory in Vision-Language-Action Systems

summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate AI research, including language-model (LM) development, offering a potential path toward recursive self-improvement. However, turning experimental feedback into a learned ability to propose effective improvements across models faces two challenges. First, training such an ability with real feedback is expensive: reinforcement learning (RL) requires evaluating tens of thousands of proposals, each potentially requiring a full model-training run. Even at ten GPU-hours per run, reward collection alone would consume hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours, motivating a cheaper surrogate. Second, surrogate feedback can become unreliable as policy optimization favors overestimated proposals when the proposal distribution shifts. To address these challenges, we propose LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL to generate effective LM improvement proposals. To provide scalable feedback, we use a research world model (RWM), a frozen LLM that predicts proposal gains from real experimental records provided in context, as the reward model for RL. To maintain feedback reliability, we periodically execute current-policy proposals ranked highly by the RWM and add their measured outcomes to its context. Across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM development environments, real-execution evaluations on held-out tasks show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform GPT-6-sol, even when GPT-6-sol is given 300 real experimental records in context, while requiring 33% lower data-generation cost. LM2LM also generalizes to a model family unseen during training.

summary: Julia code, data and result records for the article 'Sparse temporal counterfactual explanations for mixed-integer planning: recourse duality, complexity and stability'. The code computes counterfactual explanations by cost constraint generation (CCG), with dual cuts for editable recourse costs, capacity menus, period budgets and a fixed-witness stability radius, and verifies every explanation independently. The artifact holds the records of all studies: the primary study (320 runs), the external comparison (168 runs), Study 1 (256 attempts), Study 2 (1216 records), Study 3 on recourse levers (40 enumeration cases and 210 runs) and Study 4 on unit commitment (140 enumeration cases and 160 runs). The code is under the MIT license and the public input data keep their own licenses (CC BY 4.0 or Open Government Licence).

summary: R package that fits phylogenetic comparative models for continuous traits as Gaussian processes on a tree. Models are built by combining kernels (Brownian motion, Pagel's lambda, kappa and delta, early burst, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, relaxed rates, rate through time, distance-based and user-defined branch-wise kernels); the package writes and fits the corresponding Stan program, with linear-time likelihoods, leave-one-out and leave-clade-out cross-validation, prediction and ancestral-state reconstruction for branch-wise kernels, and tools to check kernel validity and equivalence.
title: phylogp: Phylogenetic Comparative Models as Gaussian Processes

summary: annotations4all is a schema-first Python library for LLM-assisted span annotation, including named entity recognition. Users define their own tag schemas; the library generates chat prompts, parses annotated model responses and maps annotations to character offsets in the original text. The library keeps annotation mechanics separate from research workflows: it bundles no corpus or fixed ontology, performs no evaluation, and does not promise model quality. Provider support uses explicit OpenAI-compatible routes rather than native SDKs. What the library provides Schema-first prompt generation and response parsing. Configurable taggers, German and English prompt templates, metadata-bearing spans and structured parser warnings. Per-label annotation and deterministic merge. Independent label runs can be combined using containment-derived hierarchy, explicit conflict reports and bounded anchoring. One request per run has a corresponding inference cost; merge is not a semantic error repair. Provider policies and capability evidence. A generic OpenAI-compatible client, provider-policy clients, explicit reasoning activation and effort, request limits, packaged hints and offline capability reports. Remote verification requires opt-in; metadata does not prove account access or successful inference. Optional read-only terminal viewer. Browse saved annotations, inspect nested spans and compare two sources using synchronized split or compact diff views. The viewer does not modify annotation files or run inference. Release notes 0.3.0 Provider-policy clients and automatic selection for documented endpoint routes; separate reasoning activation and effort, validated request conflicts, and configurable request limits. Capability reporting and packaged provider/model hints with explicit evidence boundaries. Optional Textual viewer with disjoint source selection, semantic gold-layer deduplication, split/diff views, mouse navigation, responsive legends and local diff inspection. Data-dependent contrast optimization in an isolated subprocess, opaque light/dark themes and persistent theme selection with conflict-safe settings. Deprecation warnings on construction of the old native llama.cpp and Ollama wrappers, for removal in 0.4.0. Public provider-policy clients are not deprecated. Complete versioned release notes, reproducible 160-by-48 terminal screenshots, four identical views in different themes, tests and validation scripts in the source distribution. Full 0.3 release notes and screenshots ; initial 0.2 feature baseline . Installation, documentation and verification Python 3.11 or newer. Install with pip install annotations4all==0.3.0 ; add the optional viewer with pip install 'annotations4all[view]==0.3.0' . The tutorial, API guides, release notes and screenshot provenance are included with the source archive. Verification: 982 passing tests, 92.86% coverage, Ruff lint/format checks, warning-free Markdownlint, package metadata checks and fresh-environment installation tests. Viewer checks include real optimization subprocesses and terminal restoration. These are code and packaging checks, not live-provider benchmarks. Versioning, license and citation Version 0.3.0 . summary: This report consolidates six numerical and derived consistency checks examining amplitude–phase representations of string-theory scattering within the Harmonic Physics research programme. The calculations cover two-magnon Bethe–Yang quantization in the AFS approximation (BY01), three-particle Yang–Baxter consistency for a supplied string-frame su(2|2) matrix (YB01), fundamental BES dressing-factor crossing (CP01), scalar bound-state fusion (BF01), bound-state crossing (BC01), and derived double-crossing consistency (DC01). The report presents 31 referenced equations, declared sample sets, numerical results, convergence checks and deliberately altered controls. Particular attention is given to preserving calculated amplitudes alongside phases, distinguishing coherent channel sums from scalar products, and retaining matrix-frame conventions and analytic continuation information. All six entries satisfy their declared numerical acceptance criteria. The fundamental and bound-state crossing calculations construct the continued factors independently of their target crossing equations. Double crossing is explicitly classified as a derived consistency check because its second continuation is imposed through the crossing functional equation. The accompanying reproducibility package includes the original calculation scripts, protocols, result tables, equation sources, checksums and a combined runner. A fresh integrated run successfully reproduced all five checkpoint programs covering the six entries. These results establish bounded mathematical correspondences with supplied string-theory models over the tested domains. They do not independently derive Phase dynamics, predict formation probabilities, or validate an internal nesting wavefunction. The report provides a compact equation register for carrying the supported correspondences into the broader Phase framework while preserving their provenance and limitations.

summary: Laser cladding enables bi-material components with tailored surface properties, but cyclic loading makes fatigue resistance of the whole component critical. This study examined the bending fatigue life (R = 0.1) of unalloyed steels S235J2 and S355J2 and high-strength steels S460NL and S690QL clad with aluminium bronze Metco 51NS, a combination typical of tube-bending mandrels. Results were evaluated as force amplitude versus cycles to failure using a Basquin-type power law. Fatigue strength at 10⁷ cycles was 4.0, 3.4, 3.8 and 4.5 kN, respectively, so high-strength steels performed only slightly better or similarly. Cracks always initiated on the surface of the cladding and crossed the defect-free interface. The base material is therefore not decisive for fatigue life, which is governed by the surface layer, provided cladding parameters are optimal. Less expensive unalloyed steels are thus sufficient for such components.
title: Fatigue resistance of structural steels coated with aluminium bronze using laser cladding

summary: Reproducibility bundle (artefact C4) for the paper Online Routing for Next-Action Prediction (Langiu & Pilato). Contains the full benchmark: the three corpus builders (D1 UCI Unix shell, D3 Eclipse UDC, D4 WebLINX), the seven classical pool predictors (PST, PPM, CTW leaf-KT, Lempel-Ziv, Markov-1/2/3), the three static CTW variants including the faithful binary mixture (the confirmatory baseline), the regret-bounded Hedge/Fixed-Share router, the learned GRU expert and the router-8 driver that adds it to the pool, the three negative mechanism probes with recorded decisions, the paired-statistics helper (bootstrap CI, Wilcoxon, Holm, TOST), and all seeds. Leave-one-user-out protocol. Code is MIT; the derived D4 (WebLINX) files inherit CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 from McGill-NLP/WebLINX (Lù et al. 2024); raw datasets are not redistributed and are refetchable from their public sources per the SOURCE.md files. v1.0.1 (2026-10-19): five scripts ( run_d5*.py , weight_trace.py , fewshot_llm_probe.py ) no longer carry machine-specific defaults (a local home path and a LAN endpoint); they now read D5_TRANSCRIPTS_ROOT / OLLAMA_ENDPOINT or use repository-relative paths. Data and results are unchanged.
title: cdt-prediction-bench: reproducibility bundle for Online Routing for Next-Action Prediction

Contains the full benchmark: the three corpus builders (D1 UCI Unix shell, D3 Eclipse UDC, D4 WebLINX), the seven classical pool predictors (PST, PPM, CTW leaf-KT, Lempel-Ziv, Markov-1/2/3), the three static CTW variants including the faithful binary mixture (the confirmatory baseline), the regret-bounded Hedge/Fixed-Share router, the learned GRU expert and the router-8 driver that adds it to the pool, the three negative mechanism probes with recorded decisions, the paired-statistics helper (bootstrap CI, Wilcoxon, Holm, TOST), and all seeds. Leave-one-user-out protocol. Code is MIT; the derived D4 (WebLINX) files inherit CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 from McGill-NLP/WebLINX (Lù et al. 2024); raw datasets are not redistributed and are refetchable from their public sources per the SOURCE.md files. v1.0.1 (2026-10-19): five scripts ( run_d5*.py , weight_trace.py , fewshot_llm_probe.py ) no longer carry machine-specific defaults (a local home path and a LAN endpoint); they now read D5_TRANSCRIPTS_ROOT / OLLAMA_ENDPOINT or use repository-relative paths. Data and results are unchanged.

summary: We study Independent Component Analysis (ICA) mixture models. These models consist of mixtures of ICA densities. An ICA density is associated with a random vector whose coordinates become mutually independent after an invertible linear transformation. ICA mixture models are nonparametric extensions of the celebrated family of Gaussian mixtures. We show that in many cases the ICA mixtures are identifiable from the collection of the observed moment tensors, that is, the mixing coefficients, linear transformations, and source moments of order up to $d$ can be identified from the moment tensors of order up to $d$ for generic parameters. We address the problem by studying the corresponding secant varieties and their algebraic properties such as dimensions and Gauss maps. In particular, for $n$-variate distributions, we establish that generically and up to the trivial scaling and permutation symmetries, when $d\geq 5$, the parameters can be recovered uniquely for asymptotically up to $n^{d-2}/d!$ mixture components. For $d=3,4$, we show identifiability up to a finite equivalence class for asymptotically up to $n^{d-2}/d!$ and $0.5 n^{d-2}/d!$ components respectively, where for $d=4$ the mixing coefficients need to be known a priori. The obtained bounds on the component numbers have the maximum possible orders in $n$, and for $d = 3$ and $d\geq 5$, they are also asymptotically sharp.
title: Identifiability from Moments in Independent Component Analysis Mixture Models

summary: Cross-Lingual Jailbreak Evaluation — Final Thesis Data and Outputs This archive accompanies the master's thesis Multilingual Jailbreaks in Language-Specific Large Language Models (Gabriel de Jesus Coelho da Silva; advisor Carlos Becker Westphall; Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina, 2026). It contains the study's frozen source-run files and the final thesis analysis release. The source-run files remain unchanged. The study evaluates eight instruction-tuned assistants in four language-matched pairs aligned with Portuguese, Italian, Swedish, and Bulgarian, plus a separate English reference model. StrongREJECT harmful prompts were translated into thirteen attack languages with NLLB-200, submitted to the models, and scored using the official StrongREJECT evaluator after response back-translation where applicable. The analysis combines URIEL+ featural angular distance, BELEBELE-derived IF/CONS/SPEC, and tokenizer diagnostics. The final behavioral results report the graded StrongREJECT score. The choice of this graded outcome and its fractional-logit GEE analysis followed inspection of results and was not pre-specified. Historical binary outputs remain available as provenance, not as the reported thesis results. Files added in this version File Contents final_analysis_dataset.parquet Final prompt/model/language analysis dataset, including scored responses, graded outcomes, joined predictors, coverage, and exclusion fields. final_analysis_dataset.jsonl.gz Compressed JSONL form of the same analysis release. belebele_canonical_mapping.csv Mapping of saved BELEBELE prediction rows to canonical question identities. belebele_specialization.jsonl Per-model/language IF, CONS, and SPEC from the saved generation-parsed predictions. final_analysis_supporting.zip Quality and coverage records, graded result tables and diagnostics, inference robustness analyses, translation and scoring provenance, and reported BELEBELE examples. Paths mirror the evaluation repository. README_FINAL_DATA.md , PROVENANCE.json , SHA256SUMS.txt Reading guide, source-file and archive-member provenance, and SHA-256 checksums. Frozen source-run files retained from the first version File Contents dataset_frozen.parquet Original frozen run dataset with StrongREJECT scores and historical binary labels, distance, IF/CONS/SPEC, tokenizer and translation QC fields, and exclusions. frozen_jsonl_artifacts.zip JSONL views of the original dataset and evaluator records. belebele_predictions_jsonl.zip Saved per-item generation-parsed BELEBELE predictions and original specialization summaries. tables.zip Historical binary tables and diagnostics; these are not the final graded thesis results. audit.zip LLM scalar XSTS decisions and manifests for the BLASER-flagged translation queue; these are not human judgments. translations.zip NLLB-200 prompt translations, BLASER scores, round-trip diagnostics, and recorded automatic audit decisions. configs_frozen.zip Configuration snapshot for the frozen run. model_artifacts_{MODEL_NAME}.zip Per-model generation, back-translation, scoring, and BELEBELE artifacts, including available request metadata. For the reported graded results, use the release folders under outputs/releases/2026-09-29-graded-reporting/ and outputs/releases/2026-10-16-inference-robustness/ in final_analysis_supporting.zip . The companion evaluation code is at https://github.com/gabrieljcs/ufsc-thesis (commit 4a9a84a36342f022bf99eeb1dc4e7606028bf7d4 ). PROVENANCE.json identifies the local source and SHA-256 digest for each new upload and each file inside the supporting archive. Measurement and validation limits. BELEBELE option-likelihood rescoring is specified in code but was not run for this thesis; the supplied IF/CONS/SPEC values use the generation-parsed instrument. The completed prompt QC used a BLASER gate and an uncalibrated LLM scalar audit of flagged translations. Human bilingual prompt and response audits, trusted-reference spBLEU, and MultiJail validation

summary: This dataset accompanies the manuscript Neural-network energy follows implementation, not arithmetic.   The companion code record could be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23331365 . It contains the raw measurements and processed statistics underlying the paper: raw_logs/  — original GPU-Z board-power telemetry logs (gb18030-encoded, sensor index 13) for four GPUs: RTX 3090 (all dynamic operators, NN1/NN2 training, FFN/Transformer inference, idle series), RTX A2000, UHD 770 and RTX 4080 (idle/static series). These logs are the sole measurement source of every per-operation energy in the paper. processed_statistics/  — replicate-group statistics (mean, standard deviation, count, 95% CI) for each operator underlying SI Tables S1–S7; benchmark validation data (NN1, NN2, FFN, Transformer); Arrhenius static-power fit parameters (Extended Data Fig. 1); and GPT-4 architectural reconstruction data (Extended Data Tables 1–3). source_data/  — Source Data files for every table and figure of the manuscript (Table 1, Tables S1–S9, Extended Data Tables 1–3). metadata/  — full measurement protocol (tensor shapes, batch sizes, sampling scheme, replicate-group formation) and a data dictionary for all files. Provenance:  raw logs → companion processing scripts → per-operation statistics → SI Tables S1–S7 → all manuscript figures. License:  CC-BY-4.0 .

summary: We present a geometric foundation for gravity based on a microscopic solid-angle postulate. Each mass element is assumed to exert a gravitational influence on a test mass proportional to the solid angle that the test mass subtends as seen from the element's location. For a spherically symmetric source, direct integration yields the inverse-square law without assuming Newtonian gravity---the $1/r^{2}$ behavior emerges purely from geometric dilution. Calibration with Newton's constant gives the Newtonian potential $U(r) = -GMm/r$. Combining this potential with special-relativistic energy conservation in the source rest frame leads to the exact escape velocity \[ v_{\text{esc}}(r)=c\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{\bigl(1+GM/(c^{2}r)\bigr)^{2}}}. \] The postulate is then extended to a fully covariant, causally consistent formulation in Minkowski spacetime. Using retarded interactions, we obtain for moving point masses the gravitational analogue of the Liénard--Wiechert potential, confirming that the theory respects Lorentz covariance and finite propagation speed $c$. The resulting scalar theory is formulated entirely in flat spacetime, matches Newtonian gravity in weak fields, and differs from general relativity at order $(GM/c^{2}r)^{2}$ and higher.

summary: CasADi is a symbolic framework for numeric optimization implementing automatic differentiation in forward and reverse modes on sparse matrix-valued computational graphs. It supports self-contained C-code generation and interfaces state-of-the-art codes such as SUNDIALS, IPOPT etc. It can be used from C++, Python, Matlab/Octave, Julia or Javascript
title: CasADi - A software framework for nonlinear optimization and optimal control

summary: System(3X±1)/4   Framework   for   the   Collatz (3x+1) Problem : A Definitive Proof of the Collatz Conjecture      © Dr.(Prof.) Keshava Prasad Halemane, Professor - retired (2017JAN31) from Department of Mathematical And Computational Sciences, National Institute of Technology Karnataka Surathkal, Srinivasnagar, Mangaluru - 575025, India. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3483-3521 Independent Researcher @ SASHESHA (no affiliations; no funding; no data used; no conflict of interests) https://www.linkedin.com/in/keshavaprasadahalemane/ k.prasad.h@gmail.com     Abstract   We design a mathematical framework based on System(3X±1)/4; defined similar to the Collatz (3x+1) system, with slightly modified operations.  On similar lines, we define the CTUHSK(3x+1)/4 system, and show that to be exactly the same as the Collatz (3x+1) system.  We establish the convergence of System(3X±1)/4 to its trivial-cycle {(1⇐(2)⇐4)}; using the persistent local characteristic property of ‘odd-to-odd monotonicity’ in its defining function.  We present a meticulously designed reversible (invertible) transformation (reduction); between System(3X±1)/4 and the CTUHSK(3x+1)/4 system; based on pruning-&-joining operations on the system arborescence; which does not affect the binary(inward)arborescence structure and therefore the connectedness property of either of these systems.  We establish that the transitive-closure of the subset {1,5,3} under the inverse mapping of CTUHSK(3x+1)/4 system is exactly the same as the transitive-closure of that subset under the inverse mapping of System(3X±1)/4; which has been shown to be the entire set of all natural numbers.  This establishes the convergence of the CTUHSK(3x+1)/4 system and therefore the Collatz (3x+1) system, to its trivial-cycle {(1⇐2⇐4)}; thus providing a definitive proof of the Collatz Conjecture.   This paper also presents Halemane-Conjecture on the Collatz sequence, that the upper bound on the number of odd (3x+1) operations required to reach its trivial-cycle {(1⇐2⇐4)} starting from any given positive integer and moving along the Collatz sequence, is the given number itself; the triad {(31⇐41⇐27)} being an exceptional limiting case.   Keywords: System(3X±1)/4; CTUHSK(3x+1)/4 system;          Halemane’s Conjecture on the Collatz (3x+1) system;          Collatz-Thwaites-Ulam-Hasse-Syracuse-Kakutani (CTUHSK) Sequence;          Collatz-Thwaites-Ulam-Hasse-Syracuse-Kakutani (CTUHSK) Conjecture;          binary(inward)arborescence;     AMS MSC Mathematics Subject Classification:  11B83; 11Y55; 40A99; 93A99.       Summary   System(3X±1)/4 has been defined, very similar to the Collatz (3x+1) system; with slightly modified operations.  We have also defined the CTUHSK(3x+1)/4 system, and shown that to be exactly the same as the Collatz (3x+1) system.  The convergence of System(3X±1)/4 to its trivial-cycle {(1⇐(2)⇐4)} is established using the persistent local ‘odd-to-odd monotonicity’ property of its defining function.  A reversible (invertible) transformation between System(3X±1)/4 and CTUHSK(3x+1)/4 system has been designed, based on a recursive/iterative process consisting of pruning-&-joining operations performed on the binary(inward)arborescence structure of the system.  This pruning-&-joining operation does not affect the binary(inward)arborescence structure and therefore the connectedness property of either of these systems; summary: A hydro cascade system benchmark for comparing short-term scheduling methods Frontier Falls is an eight-reservoir hydropower cascade with hourly hydrologic and electricity-market forcing, packaged as a fully specified benchmark problem. Its structure is inspired by the Cumberland River reservoir system, but all names, parameters, and operating assumptions have been modified for benchmark use —  nothing in this dataset represents actual reservoir operations, and all inflows are synthetic . Prices are public market data published by ISO New England (see  License ). The benchmark supports hydropower day-ahead scheduling studies with common physical system and shared forcing scenarios. Use cases include: Scheduling optimization  — comparing algorithms (MPC, SDDP, MILP, heuristics) on an identical, reproducible problem. Model coupling  — workflows that couple river-operations models with power-dispatch optimization. AI-agent operations  — LLM agents making bidding and release decisions with tool support. Total installed capacity: 853 MW across four storage projects and four mainstem run-of-river-style projects in a multi-river network. Detailed cascade system specifications are accompanied by five hydrologic scenarios (with 31-member ensemble 168-hour reforecasts) and five market scenarios that include day-ahead real-time (DA-RT) prices and associated reforecasts. See README.md for further details. Citing Frontier Falls Turner, S., Yu, A., Feng, J. Z., Ploussard, Q., Pavičević, M., & Galelli, S. (2026).  Frontier Falls  (version 0.9.0) [Data set]. Zenodo.  https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22680552 Machine-readable metadata is in CITATION.cff .
