summary: Small Language Models with quantisation and parameter-efficient adaptation are widely offered as the route to multilingual AI under compute constraints, and their efficiency is almost always reported as a single memory figure. We show that this figure is measured in English and does not transfer. Across a 131k-sentence corpus spanning eleven Indic scripts, TinyLlama-1.1B's tokeniser emits 1.34 subword tokens per Latin-script word and 22.60 per Kannada word. This is not inefficiency; it is absence. Its vocabulary contains 0% of Odia's codepoints, 1% of Telugu's and 2% of Kannada's, and for five of eleven scripts the measured fertility sits at the UTF-8 byte-fallback ceiling, on Odia at 99.6% of it, with 93.6% of emitted tokens being raw bytes. Because SentencePiece byte fallback never raises an unknown-token marker, this failure is entirely silent: TinyLlama's UNK rate is 0.0% on every script, including the one it reads as bytes. We further show that low fertility can indicate the opposite of efficiency: mBERT posts its best score anywhere (1.10 tokens/word, on Odia) while discarding 87.9% of the text as UNK. MuRIL, an Indic-vocabulary encoder with a fifth of TinyLlama's parameters, reads every script at 1.23-2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and zero byte fallback. The binding constraint is the vocabulary, not the parameter count. The consequence is concrete: on a 2048-token context window, the same model gives an English user 1,528 words of usable context and a Kannada user 91.
title: Efficiency Measured in English: Tokeniser Coverage Bounds Small Language Models on Indic Scripts

summary: Recent research-level physics-reasoning benchmarks for LLMs reveal a failure mode that lies not in knowledge or execution, but in modeling the world being reasoned about. Models often silently alter given quantities, fabricate laws, or inject unstated assumptions to force a problem into familiar patterns, and then reason inside this corrupted world. We define this premise-level divergence as modeling drift: the gap between a model's internal axiomatic world model (AWM) and the true physical world specified in the problem. Although RLVR and PRM have yielded substantial gains in mathematics and code, their reward shapes do not directly supervise world modeling in axiomatic domains such as physics. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Axiomatic World Modeling (RLAWM), which optimizes the policy by penalizing divergence between its inferred axiomatic world model and the true physics world. RLAWM probes physics reasoning at two hierarchical levels (modeling and solving), each scored by a physically grounded reward. The modeling reward targets abstract knowledge formulation, evaluating whether the model captures the true axiomatic world before attempting calculation. The solving reward targets instantiated knowledge reasoning, checking whether the model's concrete derivation remains consistent with the axiomatic world. This two-level structure separates what world the model believes it is reasoning in from how it reasons within that world. The framework operates exclusively during training, with no extra cost during inference. RLAWM improves performance by up to +12.2 points on PhysReason and +5.2 on PHYSICS over the baseline. It also generalizes zero-shot across difficulty, source, and domain, with a 2.45x gain and +10 points over the strongest baseline on olympiad-level physics and math.
title: Axiomatic World Modeling for Physics Reasoning

summary: Modern SAT solvers combine a rich repertoire of proof rules with sophisticated strategies that determine when and how to apply them. Often, the internal implementations are tightly coupled to particular strategies, making it inconvenient to define new strategies without changing solver internals. We present Tactix, a proof-producing sequential CDCL solver that incorporates a wide range of techniques in state-of-the-art solvers with a clean separation of proof rules from solving strategies. This separation enables a public interface through which users can invoke particular techniques, observe their effects, and program a wide range of solving strategies. The default strategy of Tactix is programmable over this interface and outperforms state-of-the-art solvers on benchmarks from the 2024--2026 SAT Competitions. We also use the interface to develop novel strategies tailored to challenging benchmarks from two application domains, which led to performance gains over strong baselines. We intend Tactix to serve as an infrastructure for designing and evaluating novel solving strategies. Finally, we also present a self-study of the AI-assisted development process behind Tactix.
title: Tactix: Towards a Programmable Strategy Interface for Flexible SAT Solving

summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can improve problem solving, but models often keep generating after the correct answer is already reachable; the extra steps raise serving costs and may replace a correct intermediate result with an incorrect one. We propose GLOBE (Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit), an online, training-free algorithm that terminates the model's CoT process early. GLOBE embeds each completed reasoning segment as a point on a unit sphere and reads the shape of the resulting semantic trajectory. GLOBE first applies a trial phase that generates short trial answers in a separate branch, stopping the main stream on an accepted trial after checking confidence against a threshold. If generation continues, a trajectory phase stops the stream once this path repeatedly reverses direction with little net progress. On five benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, tool calling, and agent memory, GLOBE cuts output tokens by 49.7% and active end-to-end wall time (E2E) by 51.0% across two models, and achieves a five-task average of 80.58%, comparable to Full CoT.
title: GLOBE: Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit via Unit-Sphere Trajectories

summary: Large language models (LLMs) are trained through multi-stage pipelines over heterogeneous data sources, yet developers lack a principled way to pinpoint the specific data responsible for an observed behavior. This lack of observability reduces debugging to reactive patching and makes failures prone to recur under distribution shift or subsequent model updates. To address this limitation, we propose DebugLM, a framework that equips LLMs with built-in data provenance, enabling them to explicitly trace the origins of their behaviors to specific training data sources. Specifically, the model learns to associate its responses with unique provenance tags that indicate the responsible dataset, empowering developers to precisely identify where undesirable behaviors are learned. Building on this capability, DebugLM further supports targeted test-time remediation, enabling developers to selectively trigger targeted refusal for specified data sources without retraining or modifying model parameters. Experiments demonstrate that DebugLM provides accurate behavior tracing in multi-stage training pipelines and effective test-time remediation while preserving the general utility of the model.
title: DebugLM: Learning Traceable Training Data Provenance for LLMs

summary: We ask how much an autoregressive transformer retains of its prompt after generating $t$ tokens. Consider two different prompts followed by the same continuation text, so that any difference in their hidden states comes from the prompt alone, and we find that the distance between their hidden states decays approximately as a power law $t^{-α}$, where $α=1$ is the rate at which a fixed prompt's share of uniform attention shrinks and smaller values mean longer memory. Trained models forget fast ($α\approx0.55$--$0.7$), untrained ones slowly ($α\approx0.2$--$0.5$). We prove that this offset is $O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big)$ for a prompt of length $P$ and depth $L$. The bound holds for finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformers with bounded attention logits, under one additional condition: the pre-norm activations stay away from zero. The mechanism is geometric: the prompt's direct influence is diluted as the context grows, and \emph{relay} --- continuation tokens passing on what earlier tokens read from the prompt --- can only add logarithmic factors. This is what we call the \emph{conditional no-hair theorem}: given the text generated so far, the prompt's influence on the next token vanishes as $t$ grows, so any property of the prompt that survives, such as its language, must be carried by the text itself. An exactly solvable linear relay model shows that the bound cannot be improved and reproduces the rise of the local exponent towards $1$ seen in untrained networks. Cancelling the dilution with a logit bias stops the decay early in training and reverses it after, so dilution is necessary for the forgetting we measure; untrained networks and the solvable model show it is also sufficient.
title: A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt

summary: Choosing features is difficult with few labeled molecules, even for a tabular foundation model that learns in context. We study this problem with TabPFN for low-data molecular property prediction, separating input width, feature meaning, and predictive usefulness while keeping contexts, query molecules, and predictor settings matched. On ADME/Tox assays from Therapeutics Data Commons, endpoint-matched assay predictions improve a compact RDKit descriptor baseline, and a provenance audit shows that most audited query molecules already occur in the predictors' training sources. Across 77 FS-Mol development tasks and 157 held-out test assays drawn from ChEMBL, broad RDKit descriptor and fingerprint families provide a strong default, rank-averaging TabPFN with support-fitted fingerprint forests improves upon both models, and learned weighting of family predictions adds further gains at a larger prediction budget. A utility-trained selector builds a traceable 16-column input from 238 sourceassay predictors, improving upon the baseline while trailing wider representations and equalwidth structural SVD coordinates. Named outputs identify what each feature predicts and where it comes from. Their usefulness for a new assay is assessed alongside the other input features, and paired removal and replacement tests measure what each selected output contributes. Together, these studies offer a protocol for evaluating feature selection, representation choice, and data provenance with a fixed tabular foundation model for few-shot molecular property prediction.
title: Feature Selection for Tabular Foundation Models: Exploring Feature Utility in Low-Data Molecular Prediction

summary: The macroscopic capabilities of intelligent systems arise from the local interactions of many simple units. When such systems are deployed in the real world, their behaviour must nevertheless be constrained, leaving designers caught between releasing adaptability and preventing loss of control, yet without formal tools to resolve the dilemma. This paper proposes a unified research program for controlled emergence that restates this tension as a pair of dual problems: the forward problem explains macroscopic behaviour from local rules, and the inverse problem solves for controllable rules and readout mechanisms from a desired target. We take an augmented quintuple as the formal object shared by both ends, and decompose ``engineering'' into three independently measurable coordinates: controllability, reproducibility, and degree of formalizability. On this basis we give three testable working hypotheses (critical scale; the cooperation and trade-off between constraint and adaptability; minimal constraint) and one feasibility criterion, which reduce inverse design from unconstrained optimization to interval checking. The program takes explicit failure boundaries as its premise, does not pursue complete control, and always preserves the system's room for self-organization. The reduced pilot experiment attached to this paper serves only to verify the executability of the research protocol and does not constitute a statistical test of the working hypotheses. This design language generalizes to multi-agent artificial intelligence, the industrial internet, and emergency response systems, all of which must confront emergence and controllability at once.
title: The Forward/Inverse Duality of Controlled Emergence:A Computational Design Program from Explanation to Engineering

summary: Model--harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the persistent yet often overlooked brain--body mismatch problem in this paradigm, where an evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses. We introduce CoEvo-RSI, a RSI framework that advances model--harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. Drawing on a shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent coordinates harness development from historical designs with model checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving execution requirements to reduce brain--body mismatch. Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. It surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant (+14.16 agent accuracy) and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM (+4.90 success rate), underscoring the need for brain--body alignment and the potential of bidirectional historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution.
title: CoEvo-RSI: When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?

summary: Open radio access network (O-RAN) enables a multi-vendor ecosystem that accelerates xApp development for near-real-time (RT) network management. However, this openness shifts a combinatorial coordination burden to the Non-RT layer, where rApp policies compose xApps from a growing catalog to realize operator intents. Coexisting intents further compound this challenge, as conflicts may arise among xApp actions, rApp policies, and their cross-layer interactions. To maximize intent admission while maintaining key performance indicator (KPI) compliance across incoming and incumbent intents, we propose a large language model-based Multi-Agentic AI framework. A Reasoning Agent screens candidate xApps against KPI contracts and produces a joint intent admission and xApp assignment decision. On post-deployment KPI violations, a Diagnosis Agent identifies the root causes of failure, labels the conflict mechanism, and guides the Reasoning Agent in subsequent attempts. Experimental results show that the framework based on GPT-OSS 120B achieves 28.6% more KPI-compliant cases and admits over 15* as many incoming intents as state-of-the-art baselines. Under the Qwen 72B variant, Diagnosis increases compliant cases by 50.0%, quadruples admitted intents, and reduces deployment attempts by 32.6%. A live deployment conforming to O-RAN specifications further validates the feasibility of the proposed solution for conflict-aware rApp policy orchestration in real networks.
title: Multi-Agentic AI for Intent-Driven and Conflict-Aware rApp Policy Orchestration in Open RAN

summary: Ranking data in modern applications often involves covariate vectors whose dimension grows with the number of objects. Identifying relevant covariates and integrating them with item-specific utilities can yield better predictive performance. In this work, we study a Plackett--Luce model that incorporates both item-specific utilities and high-dimensional covariate effects. Under a sparsity assumption on the covariate coefficients, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for identifiability in terms of the Kruskal rank of the restricted covariate design. We then propose an $\ell_1$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator for the covariate coefficients. Under suitable design and connectivity conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the estimator with probability tending to one, as well as its uniform consistency. With an additional minimum-signal condition, we further establish exact support recovery. Our analysis combines a hypergraph-based chaining technique with a profile-likelihood perturbation analysis, yielding estimation rates that explicitly capture the effects of the comparison hypergraph's connectivity and the underlying sparsity level. Numerical experiments using synthetic data and a horse racing dataset corroborate our theoretical findings.
title: High-dimensional covariate-assisted ranking

summary: Against Its Own Reverse One comparison of each binary word with its reverse builds the ring’s address, its sphere and its waveform   Driven by Dean A. Kulik October 2026   Status words. A bracket after a statement records how it stands. proved : proved in this paper. STANDS : established earlier in the series or in the literature. RUNS : an exact computation landed where the route put it, with its scope stated; every one is rerun by the scripts of Appendix B. SEALED : the prediction was written and its text hashed (SHA-256) before the computation that tests it was run; the texts and digests are in Appendix A. DEAD END : the computation ran and landed, and the landing belongs to something else, whose owner is named. OPEN : stated and not settled. PULL : an interpretive bridge, not a result. Work run in independent AI-assisted audits is marked independently . Abstract Compare every binary word with its own reverse. Write each mirrored pair of bits as a value beside a difference, the butterfly (u, u ⊕ v) taken across the mirror. The comparison is decided by the outermost pair that differs, and the Hamming weight is carried by the pairs that agree. This paper shows that the ring of all binary words is built from those two readers of one lifted word. The partner map reverses the difference half, or complements the value half when there is no difference. The address of a word is half of what lies below it plus half of the reversal pairs its own value separates, rank(p) = ½(p − π(p) + Δ(p)) + π c (p), where Δ(p) = #{x : x < p ≤ J(x)} has a closed digit form and grows by a borrow chain whose cell is the full adder’s carry with one input complemented; the first 64 bits of π land at 2,427,008,858,123,944,441 from one pass over the 32 bits of each half. The route that grows a word one bit at a time is the lift itself: its residual bits are the mirrored differences, innermost first. On the sphere of radius n and latitude z = wt − n/2, latitude reads only the agreeing pairs, so the poles belong to the palindromes and a word with k disagreeing pairs stays within |z| ≤ ⌊n/2⌋ − k + [n odd]/2; the partner is a reflection, and on palindromes a half-turn about the X-axis. On ring addresses the partner is the complement of the address, so the latitude splits into a Walsh-even body and a Walsh-odd palindrome carrier whose energy share is exactly 2 1−n/2 at even width. Pulled back, each reader is simple in its own coordinates and spread in the other’s: over the bits of a word the comparison needs 2(2 ⌊ n/2 ⌋ − 1) Walsh modes and the latitude n; over ring addresses the comparison is one address bit carrying 99.9% of its energy at n = 20, while the latitude fills 1,036,432 of 1,048,576 modes. The ring is the coordinate system of the comparison. How the paper runs The paper is written from its end. summary: Run records, logs, analyses and binding-event replica trajectories of the streptavidin : fibril ratio sweep simulated by Team Imperial College (iGEM 2026, Imperial College London) with HyFiP-LDF, our open-source coarse-grained HOOMD-blue 7.2.0 Langevin-dynamics model of a protein hydrogel (HET-s(218–289) amyloid fibrils end-labelled with maleimide–PEG–biotin linkers and crosslinked by streptavidin tetramers). The sweep covers six streptavidin : fibril ratios (1/6, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 3/2, 3) at three random seeds each, 105 ns per run at surrogate conditions (75 nm fibrils, ten times the wet-lab number density, friction scaled by 0.1, 300 nm periodic box), run on one NVIDIA RTX 5090. 13 of 18 runs finished; the configurations and partial logs of the 5 stopped runs are included. Also included are the 52 re-simulations of one binding event (restarted from saved frames with new random seeds at 2 ps resolution) used to study how a biotin finds a streptavidin pocket. For every run: the complete resolved configuration, a run manifest with software versions and every model parameter with its provenance and data-file hashes, the HOOMD energy and temperature log, and the network, thermodynamic and structural analyses. These are the data behind Figures 26–28 and Videos 4–5 of the Simulations page of our wiki. Software: https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/software/imperial-college/cg-langevin-simulation (Apache-2.0). Atomistic reference data: 10.5281/zenodo.23420371. See README.md inside the archive for the file layout, variables, units and methods.

summary: annotations4all is a schema-first Python library for LLM-assisted span annotation, including named entity recognition. Users define their own tag schemas; the library generates chat prompts, parses annotated model responses and maps annotations to character offsets in the original text. The library keeps annotation mechanics separate from research workflows: it bundles no corpus or fixed ontology, performs no evaluation, and does not promise model quality. Provider support uses explicit OpenAI-compatible routes rather than native SDKs. What the library provides Schema-first prompt generation and response parsing. Configurable taggers, German and English prompt templates, metadata-bearing spans and structured parser warnings. Per-label annotation and deterministic merge. Independent label runs can be combined using containment-derived hierarchy, explicit conflict reports and bounded anchoring. One request per run has a corresponding inference cost; merge is not a semantic error repair. Provider policies and capability evidence. A generic OpenAI-compatible client, provider-policy clients, explicit reasoning activation and effort, request limits, packaged hints and offline capability reports. Remote verification requires opt-in; metadata does not prove account access or successful inference. Optional read-only terminal viewer. Browse saved annotations, inspect nested spans and compare two sources using synchronized split or compact diff views. The viewer does not modify annotation files or run inference. Release notes 0.3.1 Request pacing now resolves symlinks in the parent directories of the per-user state file, so a symlinked cache root no longer fails every paced request. The state file keeps its no-follow, regular-file and ownership protection, and cross-process locking is unchanged. Documentation is available in both languages: tutorial and viewer guide each in German and English. Release 0.3.0 introduced provider-policy clients, capability reporting, the optional viewer, data-dependent contrast optimization and deprecation warnings for the legacy native wrappers; the 0.3 notes remain the reference for that feature set. 0.3.1 release notes ; 0.3 feature release notes and screenshots ; initial 0.2 feature baseline . Installation, documentation and verification Python 3.11 or newer. Install with pip install annotations4all==0.3.1 ; add the optional viewer with pip install 'annotations4all[view]==0.3.1' . The tutorial in German and English, the API guides, release notes and screenshot provenance are included with the source archive. Verification: 984 passing tests, 92.8% coverage, Ruff lint/format checks, warning-free Markdownlint, package metadata checks and fresh-environment installation tests under Python 3.11 and 3.13. Viewer checks include real optimization subprocesses and terminal restoration. These are code and packaging checks, not live-provider benchmarks. Versioning, license and citation Version 0.3.1 . summary: NOTE: 1. The R package to compute NPP from brGDGTs is available in https://github.com/MarcoVidalCordasco/envirolipids  2.  R_Code_and_Analysis_Guide.pdf facilitates navigation through the analytical workflow and helps identifying the code associated with each result presented in the study.  ## 📌 Overview This repository contains an R workflow for analysing branched GDGT (brGDGT) compounds and modelling **Net Primary Productivity (NPP)** using statistical and machine learning approaches. It also includes the full ecological modelling workflow to recosntruct herbivore biomass and carrying capacity of secondary consumers. There are two scripts: * Script_1 * Script_2 The Script_1 performs: * Exploratory data analysis * Statistical modelling (linear, quadratic, GAM) * Random Forest modelling with three validation strategies * Independent dataset validation * NPP reconstruction from Padul-15-05 core * Comparison with climate-derived NPP (Miami model) * Summed Probability Distribution (SPD) analysis for archaeological data * Correlation analysis * Summary statistics and plots The Script_2 performs: * Herbivore density estimations from primary productivity * Population structure modelling using survival curves * Biomass partitioning across body size classes * Secondary consumers carrying capacity calculations * Summary statistics and plots --- ## 📂 Data Requirements The Script_1 expects an Excel file: ``` Dataset_1.xlsx This contains: * A global dataset of present-day measured brGDGTs and associated climatic, edaphic and environmental variables * Areas with in-field NPP measurements * Climate conditions reconstructed in Padul * Archaeological sites, levels and dates for the summed probability distributions ``` The Script_2 expects two additional Excel files: ``` Dataset_2.xlsx This contains: * Herbivore traits (species, body mass, life history traits, etc.), * The wild mammal species list recovered in the region during the Late Pleistocene and Early Holocene (including sites and references) * NPP values (actual and potential) obtained from Script_1 * Primary and secondary consumer biomass summaries ``` ``` Prey_preferences.xlsx This contains: * Predator diet composition and annual biomass requirements ``` ## 📦 R Packages A package to apply the random-forest NPP predictions from brGDGTs is under construction --- ## ⚠️ Notes * Ensure working directory is set correctly: ```r setwd(dirname(rstudioapi::getActiveDocumentContext()$path)) ``` * All files available in this repository should be saved into the same folder/directory --- ## 📬 Contact # mav54#cam.ac.uk

summary: Example data to reproduce the BAGFOOT2 protocol and vignette: mouse liver ATAC-seq, Fed vs Fasted (3 replicates per condition, mm10). BAGFOOT2 predicts which transcription factors change their activity between two conditions from ATAC-seq data, by combining Tn5 bias-corrected footprint depth and flanking accessibility over archetype motif clusters, with a robust Mahalanobis distance (MCD) test. Files bam_merged.tar.gz: one merged, sorted and indexed BAM file per condition (fed, fasted) bam_replicates.tar.gz: one BAM file per replicate (fed_1-3, fasted_1-3), used for HOMER (large file) tag_directories.tar.gz: HOMER tag directories of the replicates (TD_fed_1 ... TD_fasted_3) macs2.tar.gz: MACS2 peak calls (narrowPeak) per condition bg_files_fed_fasted.tar.gz: BAGFOOT2 (v2.0.0) output for Fed vs Fasted (bagplot, D2 and FDR barplots, result table) The motif database files (mm10, hg38) are NOT in this record. They are downloaded automatically by BAGFOOT2 on first use, from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20782782 How to reproduce Install BAGFOOT2: conda create -n bagfoot2 -c goldsteinlab-tech -c conda-forge -c bioconda bagfoot2 Extract the archives into one project folder: fed_fasted/bam_merged/ (merged BAM files, replicate BAM files and tag directories) fed_fasted/macs2/ (peak files) Run: bagfoot2 -b fed_fasted/bam_merged/ -p fed_fasted/macs2/ -o bg_files_fed_fasted/ -c fed -t fasted -g mm10 --bam_suffix ".sorted.bam" --cores 4 Add --homer TRUE --homer_bin /path/to/homer/bin --reps_control 1,2,3 --reps_treatment 1,2,3 to include HOMER motif enrichment. Code: https://github.com/goldsteinlab-tech/BAGFOOT2 Documentation: https://goldsteinlab-tech.github.io/BAGFOOT2/ RELATED WORKS Is supplement to: https://github.com/goldsteinlab-tech/BAGFOOT2 (Software) References: 10.5281/zenodo.20782782 (Dataset, motif database)

summary: This repository contains the replication materials accompanying the research note Financial Pessimism and the Timing of Saving (Alexander Hansak, University of Graz, 2026). The archive includes the original Python analysis, an independent R implementation of the principal estimators and survey-design standard errors, supplementary empirical analyses, Julia preprocessing scripts, questionnaire documentation, and aggregate estimation results. The canonical Python replay and independent R implementation reproduce 21 reported coefficient and standard-error comparisons on identical model-ready samples. Additional analyses examine saving amounts, subsequent income and employment outcomes, and age heterogeneity. All nine supplementary verification stages passed. The additional empirical specifications have not been independently cross-implemented. The analysis uses the British Household Panel Survey (BHPS) and Understanding Society (UKHLS), distributed through UK Data Service study 6614 (DOI: 10.5255/UKDA-SN-6614-22). Licensed respondent-level data are not redistributed. Researchers wishing to reproduce the analysis must obtain authorized access to the original survey data. The archive provides source code, execution instructions, numerical verification reports, aggregate outputs, and SHA-256 integrity manifests. The empirical findings describe conditional associations rather than identified causal effects. Version: 1.1.0 (20 October 2026).

summary: annotations-orchestration is a Python library for configuring and running LLM annotation and evaluation experiments. It combines a resumable, manifest-driven scheduler with an optional terminal editor and a declarative annotation runner. Span metrics are computed by annotations-evaluate ; annotation clients, taggers, provider capabilities and hints come from annotations4all . Scope and architecture Base scheduler: experiment YAMLs and optional controller manifests define runs, defaults, execution settings and ordering. The default legacy runner uses a subprocess CLI contract and does not require an annotation library. Optional editor: the tui extra provides annotations-tui , a Textual editor for single-run and multi-run experiments and controllers. Editing, inspection and effective-run previews do not execute experiments. Optional standard runner: the annotate extra uses annotations4all>=0.3.1,<1 to annotate from a declarative annotation block without a custom consumer frontend. Metrics: this package adapts run records and writes reports; it does not implement metric counting. Run reports use the SemEval-compatible flat scenarios of annotations-evaluate ; that library also provides a nested standard report. Release notes 0.3.0 This release adds the editor, standard runner and provider-aware configuration layer to the 0.2 scheduler.
